clue.text: Subjects such as History, English, Classics on ice regrettably

indicators.note: what happens regrettably goes wrong, so the letters end up in a mangled order

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
the letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lament about humanities subjects being put on ice, sadly shelved by some institution.
explanation.walkthrough: The list 'History, English, Classics' looks like one run of examples, but only 'History' belongs to the definition; English is the single letter E feeding the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: History is one of the academic disciplines studying human society, so it serves as an example of that group of subjects.

clue.text: Arise in plane, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: come up, emerge into view
second meaning: a flat plane is one kind of this, as in geometry

explanation.surface: Something climbing upward inside an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' suggests an aircraft taking off, but here it is the flat geometric figure; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb meaning to come up to the top, and as a noun for an outer face, of which a geometric plane is one kind.

clue.text: Ice creams consumed by deaconess

indicators.note: what is consumed sits inside the eater, so the letters lie buried within a longer word

blocks.note: the letters sit inside dea-...-s

explanation.surface: A church deaconess tucking into ice creams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumed' fits the eating picture perfectly, which is what hides its role as the signal to look inside the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice creams are commonly served in wafer cones, and a cone is a single ice cream in everyday British use.

clue.text: A nation with naval strength, we're told: it's in the mains

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a country strong at sea is a sea power

explanation.surface: Talk of a maritime nation whose strength lies in the 'main', the old poetic word for the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The mains' plays on 'the main', the sea; it actually means the household electricity supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Household electricity supplied through the mains is alternating current, abbreviated AC, so that power flows in the mains.

clue.text: The queen to cross parting water (that is, lake), finding dog

blocks.note: a spring is water issuing, or parting, from the ground
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen
to span is to cross from one side to the other
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A monarch crossing water, like Moses parting the sea, and coming across a dog by a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces do not come in clue order: the water comes first, then the queen, then the crossing; the parenthesis simply supplies the last two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a breed of gundog, a lively spaniel originally used to flush, or spring, game birds.

clue.text: The writer had 50 hesitant expressions: they won't work

blocks.note: the writer is the setter, I, and 'I had' contracts to I'd
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
'er' is the sound people make when hesitating

explanation.surface: An author umming and erring fifty times, the sort of filler words that never pull their weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the crossword convention for the setter, so it gives I, and with 'had' the contraction I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Lazy people who avoid labour are loafers, so a plural noun for those who refuse to graft fits the phrase exactly.

clue.text: Cold spot, Norway: the European's replaced by another

indicators.note: replacing swaps one thing out, so a part is exchanged for something else of the same kind

blocks.note: the country's name comes from 'north way', and it is the northern land
the Norwegian, the person from that country, who is the part swapped out
another European: a native of Poland, swapped in for the Norwegian

explanation.surface: A frosty Norwegian location where one European is swapped for another.
explanation.walkthrough: Think of Norway as 'north' plus a Norwegian; replace the Norwegian with a different European, a Pole, and the two parts join up.
explanation.definitionFit: The northernmost point on Earth sits amid permanent Arctic ice, making it about the coldest place anyone could name.

clue.text: Being somewhat high-minded, I blessed foodstuffs

indicators.note: 'somewhat' means only partly, so just part of the following text is taken

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and stops inside the last

explanation.surface: A lofty-minded person saying grace over the food.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the hyphen and comma: the letters run straight through 'mind-ed, I bless-ed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Things fit to eat are foodstuffs; the plural noun is a common if slightly informal word for items of food.

clue.text: Primarily Islamic republic, Azerbaijan's neighbour?

indicators.note: 'primarily' means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A quiz-style question about a mainly Muslim state bordering Azerbaijan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' reads as 'mainly Islamic', but it picks out first letters; the whole clue then doubles as the description of the country.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is officially an Islamic Republic and shares a long northern border with Azerbaijan, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: '80s ballad that's ornate was fast enthralling one

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one part holds another inside it

blocks.note: purple prose is overly ornate writing
ran: moved quickly
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A florid 1980s ballad that once held listeners spellbound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ornate' gives the colour through the phrase 'purple prose'; the numeral one then sits inside the past tense of run.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince's 1984 song is a famous power ballad from that decade, title track of his album and film.

clue.text: C. European city, in retrospect, used to be chilly

indicators.note: looking in retrospect means looking back, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: past tense of be
raw weather is cold and damp

explanation.surface: Someone recalling that a central European city was once cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The two past-and-weather words are joined first and only then the whole string turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polish capital lies in central Europe; 'C.' is simply the abbreviation for Central.

clue.text: Oddly, loner awash, swimming with toothy mammals

indicators.note: 'oddly' points to the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth
things swimming move about freely, so the letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A solitary creature adrift in the sea, swimming alongside some sharp-toothed beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the odd letters of the first word go into the mix, along with all of 'awash'.
explanation.definitionFit: These Arctic whales are known for the male's single long spiral tusk, which is an enormously elongated tooth.

clue.text: Great Dane cavorting in genteel eatery

indicators.note: cavorting means leaping about wildly, so the letters jump out of place

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A huge dog bounding around a refined cafe.
explanation.walkthrough: The breed name is just raw letters; the dog's antics are the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor cafe serving tea and cakes is a refined, old-fashioned place to eat, hence a well-mannered restaurant.

clue.text: It's used for pumping reggae with sun out

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or askew, so the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Music pumping out of a sound system, with reggae playing once the sun has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like 'sun out' meaning sunshine, but it signals rearranging the music and the star together.
explanation.definitionFit: This workshop tool forces lubricant into machine fittings under pressure, so pumping is exactly its job.

clue.text: Scoffs wines, spirits etc loudly

indicators.note: something said loudly is heard aloud, so the spoken sound counts

blocks.note: booze is alcoholic drink in general

explanation.surface: Someone noisily guzzling all the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffs' suggests gobbling food or drink; here it means jeers at, a verb matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff at someone is to mock or jeer, and to boo is to jeer noisily, so both are third-person verbs of derision.

clue.text: Pint? Regularly bleary, Everyman's beginning to tuck in

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
a beginning is the start, so only the opening letter is wanted
to tuck something in is to slip it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
the setter's name, first letter

explanation.surface: A bleary-eyed setter about to tuck into a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the name of this puzzle series, so its first letter is slipped inside the alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In a British pub a pint, by default, means a pint glass of this drink, so the measure stands for it.

clue.text: Corroborate order to get some distance from Paddington?

definitions.text: order to get some distance from Paddington?

blocks.note: first meaning: confirm, support a claim

blocks.clueFragment: order to get some distance from Paddington?
blocks.note: second meaning: a command telling the famous storybook animal to leave

explanation.walkthrough: Paddington sounds like the London railway station, so 'distance from Paddington' suggests a journey; really Paddington is the bear from Michael Bond's children's books, being told to get out.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm evidence is to support or back it up; the phrasal verb is a standard idiom for that.

clue.text: Beautiful princess with roly-poly dessert: very excited!

indicators.note: roly-poly suggests rolling over, and something rolled over ends up back to front

blocks.note: Psyche, in Greek myth, was a princess so lovely that Eros fell for her
pud is British slang for pudding, i.e. dessert

explanation.surface: A lovely princess thrilled at the sight of a jam roly-poly pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Jam roly-poly is a British rolled sponge pudding, so 'roly-poly' looks like the dessert's name but tells you to roll it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Being mentally geared up and eager before an event is a common idiom for strong excitement or readiness.

clue.text: Lectures caught by young women

indicators.note: 'by' means next to, so one piece sits beside the other

blocks.note: c. is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
lasses are girls, in Scottish and northern English use

explanation.surface: Talks that a group of girls happened to catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught by' reads as a passive verb, but 'caught' is just the cricket abbreviation placed beside the girls.
explanation.definitionFit: Teaching sessions in a course are interchangeable with talks given by a tutor, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Show half of mum's brothers having left

indicators.note: half means only part is kept and the rest is dropped

blocks.note: uncles, cut to the first three of six letters
what is left is left over

explanation.surface: Mum's brothers, half of whom have already gone home from a family show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like departed; here it is 'left over', remaining.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something by taking away what hides it is to display it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: You should see Papa before seeing this city!

definitions.text: You should see Papa before seeing this city!

blocks.clueFragment: You should see Papa before seeing this city!
blocks.note: surface reading: advice to visit your father before a trip to some city
setter's reading: Papa is the NATO phonetic code word for P, and the code word for the next letter is also a Canadian city

explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet each letter has a code word; the word for the letter after P is also the name of a city in Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-speaking Canadian city, capital of its province, shares its name with the radio code word for Q.

clue.text: Ale container, a large piece of brass

blocks.note: Bass is a well-known English brand of pale ale
a tub is a container
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beer vessel, a big brass object like a pub tankard or plaque.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests the metal or money; it means the brass section of a band.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lowest-pitched member of the brass family of instruments, and a physically big one.

clue.text: Somewhere in France, piece of offal's acerbic

indicators.note: a piece is just a portion, so only a stretch of the following text is taken

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A French diner finding a bit of offal sharp-tasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of offal' reads as a kidney or liver; it signals taking a run of letters across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a region in north-eastern France on the German border, so it is a place in that country.

clue.text: Abandon in brushwood

blocks.note: first meaning: cancel, drop a plan
second meaning: stunted trees and shrubs

explanation.surface: Someone left behind in the undergrowth.
explanation.walkthrough: The informal sense of calling off a plan is the one solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the verb means to cancel or call off, while the noun means low scrubland vegetation of bushes.

clue.text: Good old pancakes, finally disappeared inside cookers: frightful apparitions

indicators.note: the final one has disappeared, so the last letter is removed
inside means within, so one part goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
O is the abbreviation for old
blini are small Russian pancakes, with the last letter dropped
a hob is a cooktop, the British word for a stove top

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned pancakes vanishing into the ovens, as if spirited away by ghosts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good old' looks like a fond phrase but is two separate abbreviations; together with the shortened pancakes they go inside the cookers.
explanation.definitionFit: These mischievous goblin-like creatures of folklore are frightening spirits, so scary phantoms is a fair description.

clue.text: Extravagant praise for dance party

blocks.note: first meaning: a glowing review
second meaning: a large all-night event with electronic music

explanation.surface: A glowing write-up of a club night.
explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings are nouns: a rave review, and a big electronic music event.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both an enthusiastic review and a large all-night event with electronic music, as in 1990s club culture.

clue.text: Sees bronco told off on the wagon

indicators.note: something off is not right, so these letters are out of their proper order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cowboy watches an unruly wild horse get scolded beside a wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told off' reads as scolded, but 'told' is fodder and 'off' the signal; 'on the wagon' is the idiom for abstaining from alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the wagon has given up alcohol, so they are completely free of drink, utterly sober.
